title: Neyman–Pearson lemma as a named UMP slogan
dek: Simple H0 vs simple H1: the likelihood-ratio test is most powerful. Composite nested LRTs are a different theorem (Wilks).
story: The Neyman–Pearson lemma on Wikipedia is a simple-versus-simple result: among tests of a given size, the likelihood-ratio rejection region maximises power. It is the slogan behind 'why likelihood ratios'.
Composite hypotheses (free parameters, nested GLMs) are not this lemma. That is Wilks / Karlin–Rubin / scores. Do not cite NP 1933 for a 4-df LRT in a TB GLM.
Type I/II language sits on a sibling card. Power as a design object is stats-power.
deep: Simple means fully specified densities, no leftover θ.
One-sided tests with MLR can still have UMP (Karlin–Rubin); two-sided often do not.
p-values are a later reporting culture, not the 1933 lemma itself.
Diagnostic LRs (Se/(1−Sp)) rhyme with NP but are not a hypothesis test.

visual.caption: Two fully specified densities. NP says reject where their ratio is large. Composite nested tests are a different picture (wiki-wilks).
